scenes.title: Presidential Election Odds
scenes.narration_text: Your chance of deciding a presidential election: one in sixty million. You're more likely to die in a car crash driving to the polls.
scenes.context: Comparing the astronomical odds of a single vote affecting an election to more common risks.

scenes.title: Value of a Vote
scenes.narration_text: The expected value of your vote is zero point zero zero zero one seven dollars. The cost of casting it (time, gas, parking) is about fifty dollars.
scenes.context: The speaker contrasts the negligible financial worth of a single vote with the high cost of voting.

scenes.title: Mathematical Meaninglessness
scenes.narration_text: Democracy was designed so that your individual participation is mathematically meaningless. What isn't meaningless:
scenes.context: Defining the core design of democracy regarding individual influence vs. collective math.

scenes.title: Lobbying Billions
scenes.narration_text: the four point one billion dollars corporations spend annually on lobbying. That math works out just fine.
scenes.context: Highlighting the massive scale of corporate spending that actually influences policy.

scenes.title: Founding Fathers' Oversight
scenes.narration_text: The Founding Fathers were brilliant men. They anticipated tyranny, corruption, foreign invasion, and mob rule. They did not anticipate Florida.
scenes.context: The founders planned for major crises but failed to foresee modern political absurdity.

scenes.title: Policy Decision Analysis
scenes.narration_text:
What Democracy Should Look Like versus Reality.

Princeton University analyzed one thousand seven hundred and seventy-nine policy decisions
scenes.context: Introducing a major study comparing actual policy outcomes with public intent.

scenes.title: Zero Voter Influence
scenes.narration_text: over twenty years. The correlation between what ordinary voters want and what actually happens? Zero. Percent.
scenes.context: Revealing the stark lack of connection between voter desires and legislative reality.

scenes.title: Economic Elites' Power
scenes.narration_text:
When economic elites want something? Seventy-eight percent of the time.

You have the same political influence as your houseplant.
scenes.context: Contrasting the influence of elites with that of the average voter.

scenes.title: Influence of a Houseplant
scenes.narration_text: Slightly less, actually. Your houseplant produces oxygen, which at least one congressman needs.
scenes.context: A cynical comparison about the relative utility of a voter versus a plant.

scenes.title: Ironic Department Names
scenes.narration_text: Your institutions tell the whole story in their names. You have a "Department of Defense" that mainly attacks people.
scenes.context: Critiquing the naming conventions of government departments versus their actions.

scenes.title: Defensive and Health Ironies
scenes.narration_text: A "Department of Health" that has not yet produced any observable health. And a "Department of Justice" that (you can see where this is going).
scenes.context: Further examples of departments failing to live up to their stated missions.

scenes.title: Passing Odds
scenes.narration_text: Whether zero percent or one hundred percent of voters support a bill, it has the same about thirty percent chance of passing.
scenes.context: Showing that public support has no statistical effect on a bill's success.

scenes.title: Democracy Slot Machine
scenes.narration_text: Democracy is a slot machine where every pull gives the same result but you keep playing because the machine has an American flag on it.
scenes.context: Comparing the democratic process to a rigged gambling game adorned with patriotic symbols.

scenes.title: Political Failure Math
scenes.narration_text:
The Mathematics of Political Failure.

Concentrated Benefits versus Diffuse Costs.

Sugar subsidies cost Americans three point five billion dollars

per year. That's ten dollars per person.

scenes.narration_text:

Banks in two thousand and eight received a seven hundred billion dollar bailout (concentrated).

How Money Buys Power.

scenes.context: Explaining that political influence is more complex than simple vote-buying.

scenes.title: Rich Country Bribery
scenes.narration_text:
Bribery is what poor countries do. Rich countries have "campaign finance."

But they do something far more effective:
scenes.context: The speaker contrasts crude bribery with the legalized 'campaign finance' of developed nations.

scenes.narration_text:
they buy which politicians exist in the first place.

Ninety-five percent of House races since two thousand and four were won by the highest spender.
scenes.context: Revealing that the primary function of money is selecting who gets to run for office.

scenes.title: Cost of Winning
scenes.narration_text:

The average winning Senate campaign costs twenty-six point five three

scenes.narration_text:
million dollars.

when you own the restaurant.

scenes.context: The speaker moves from candidate selection to how incumbents are influenced.

Agenda control. Your issue gets a hearing, theirs gets buried.

You don't buy the vote. You buy the voter, the agenda, and the room where the vote happens.
scenes.context: Summary of how lobbying controls the entire environment of governance.

scenes.context: A comparison is made between the effectiveness of lobbyists and the funding received for different diseases.

scenes.title: Allocation of Resources
scenes.narration_text:
Rare pediatric diseases have no lobbyists and therefore receive no funding.

Democracy doesn't allocate resources by who's dying.
scenes.context: The narrator explains the harsh reality of how funding is allocated in a lobbyist-driven democracy.

scenes.narration_text: It allocates by who can afford the best lobbyist. If your disease can't hire a P.R. firm, it's not a real disease. It's just dying.
scenes.context: The narrator cynically notes that without public relations, a disease is ignored by the system.

scenes.title: Fundraising Congressman
scenes.narration_text:
Your Congressman: A Fundraiser Who Occasionally Legislates.

The average congressman spends four hours a day on fundraising.
scenes.context: The text moves to a new section describing the daily routine and primary focus of members of Congress.

scenes.title: Reading Bills vs Governing
scenes.narration_text:
The average congressman spends zero hours a day reading bills.

Actual governing is whatever time is left.

They don't read what they vote on.
scenes.context: The narrator highlights that congressmen do not actually read the legislation they pass.

scenes.title: Speed Reading Legislation
scenes.narration_text: The Patriot Act was three hundred and forty-two pages, voted on forty-five minutes after release. That's seven point six pages per minute.
scenes.context: An example of the impossible speed at which the Patriot Act was processed after its release.

scenes.title: The ACA Passing
scenes.narration_text: Olympic speed-readers can't do that. The Affordable Care Act was twenty-seven hundred pages, and the famous quote was "we have to pass it to see what's in it".
scenes.context: The narrator mocks the legislative process using the example of the Affordable Care Act's massive page count.

scenes.title: Committees Control
scenes.narration_text:
These people control nuclear weapons. Sleep tight.

Congressional Committees: The Menu.

Committees control which bills live or die.
scenes.context: Transitioning to a new section about the power and corruption inherent in congressional committees.

scenes.title: Fundraising Quotas
scenes.narration_text: Both parties assign fundraising quotas for each seat: raise this much for the party, or lose your assignment.
scenes.context: Explaining the financial requirements imposed on congressmen to keep their committee positions.

scenes.title: Wall of Shame
scenes.narration_text: Don't hit your number? Your bills die, your amendments vanish, and your name goes on a literal "wall of shame".
scenes.context: Describing the consequences for congressmen who fail to meet their party's fundraising targets.

scenes.title: Buying Sections
scenes.narration_text:
It's like a restaurant where the waiters have to pay for their own sections.

Here's the menu. Want to be House Speaker?
scenes.context: Using a restaurant metaphor to introduce the 'price list' for specific political positions.

scenes.title: Price for Speaker
scenes.narration_text: Raise twenty to thirty-one million dollars for your party. Want to chair a powerful committee like Ways and Means or Appropriations?
scenes.context: The specific millions required to obtain the House Speaker position or a powerful chair.

scenes.title: Powerful Committee Costs
scenes.narration_text: That'll cost you about one point two to one point eight million dollars in party fundraising.
scenes.context: The narrator specifies the cost of chairing the most influential committees in Congress.

scenes.title: Entry Fee Table

For the House Speaker position,

scenes.context: Breaking down the specific fundraising requirement for a Democratic House Speaker.

scenes.narration_text: and the National Republican Congressional Committee, or N.R.C.C., requires twenty million dollars because the Speaker controls the entire agenda.
scenes.context: Explaining the Republican Speaker's cost and the reason for the high price tag.

scenes.narration_text:
and Republicans must raise one point two million dollars.

For the Appropriations Chair, which controls the one point seven trillion dollar budget,
scenes.context: Listing the price for Republicans on tax committees and the introduction to budget committee costs.

scenes.narration_text: Democrats must raise one point eight million dollars and Republicans must raise one point two million dollars.
scenes.context: The specific fundraising totals required to lead the Appropriations committee.

scenes.title: Energy and Commerce Cost
scenes.narration_text: For Energy and Commerce, covering healthcare, energy, and telecommunications, Democrats must raise one point eight million dollars
scenes.context: Detailing the price of power over healthcare, energy, and tech sectors.

scenes.title: Regular Committee Price
scenes.narration_text:
and Republicans must raise one point two million dollars.

A Regular Committee seat costs between five hundred thousand and one million dollars
scenes.context: The narrator continues listing the tiered pricing for various congressional responsibilities.

scenes.context: A final look at the pricing for standard committee seats in the two major parties.

scenes.title: The Rent for Power
scenes.narration_text:
A Basic Member owes at least one hundred and fifty thousand dollars as the entry fee to play.

This is why congressmen spend four hours a day fundraising.
scenes.context: Connecting the financial quotas back to why politicians spend so much time on the phone with donors.

scenes.context: The narrator explains that political positions are essentially purchased by the industries they oversee.

scenes.context: The core thesis of Public Choice Theory: government workers remain human and fallible.

scenes.title: Selfish Bureaucrats
scenes.narration_text: bureaucrats, politicians, and regulators are just as selfish as everyone else.
scenes.context: The text asserts that public servants are motivated by the same self-interests as the general public.

scenes.title: Greed Differences
scenes.narration_text: The only difference is that when a corporation is greedy, you can stop buying their product.
scenes.context: A distinction is made between market-based greed and state-based power.

scenes.title: Bureaucracy vs Corporation
scenes.narration_text:

What They Actually Maximize.
scenes.context: The narrator highlights the coercive power of the state compared to private companies.

scenes.title: NIH Grant Maximization
scenes.narration_text: The N.I.H. should maximize cures, but actually maximizes grants awarded, resulting in no cures.
scenes.context: An application of Public Choice Theory showing why the NIH fails to produce results despite funding.

scenes.title: FDA Lawsuit Avoidance
scenes.narration_text: The F.D.A. should maximize lives saved, but actually maximizes avoiding lawsuits, resulting in deadly delays.
scenes.context: The author critique the misaligned priorities of regulatory agencies.

scenes.title: Congress & Donations
scenes.narration_text: Congress should maximize voter welfare, but actually maximizes campaign donations, resulting in corporate welfare.
scenes.context: The critique shifts to the legislative branch and the influence of campaign finance.

scenes.title: Pharma & Chronic Disease
scenes.narration_text: Pharma should maximize health outcomes, but actually maximizes recurring revenue, meaning chronic disease is preferred.
scenes.context: Analysis of how pharmaceutical companies prioritize profit over cures.

scenes.title: Defense Contracts
scenes.narration_text: Defense contractors should maximize national security, but actually maximize government contracts, resulting in endless wars.
scenes.context: The author discusses the incentives driving the military-industrial complex.

scenes.title: The Gandhi Clone
scenes.narration_text: Nobody in the system is incentivized to cure disease. Or end war. You could elect five hundred and thirty-five clones of Gandhi
scenes.context: The author argues that individual virtue cannot overcome systemic corruption.

scenes.title: Systemic Digestion
scenes.narration_text: and within two years they'd be taking pharma money. The system digests idealists like a stomach digests food.
scenes.context: Explaining how the political system corrupts even the most idealistic individuals.

scenes.narration_text: Public Choice Theory says government fails because the people running it are people, and people are terrible.
scenes.context: Explaining the academic theory that views political actors as self-interested individuals.

scenes.title: Selfish Systems
scenes.narration_text: The solution is to stop expecting people to be good and design systems where being selfish accidentally produces good outcomes,
scenes.context: Proposing a design-based solution to systemic human selfishness.

scenes.narration_text: Everyone who's dying loses. The system works perfectly. It's just optimized for the wrong thing.
